en: And his many sworn enemies
Renounced not only their livestock
But even their lives entirely.
It was then that brave Seytek,
Questioning his uncle,
Entered the mountain fastness
And became embroiled in a great
And incurable tumult.
He entered a calamity that would not subside,
And became embroiled in a dispute.
“My precious uncle, bloodthirsty lion,
Sing and tell your song;
Tell your truth as solemnly as your creed.
Uncle, reveal your secret.
While your fortune was unharmed,
While your gray-wolf uncle lived,
You reached Afghanistan and raided it.
If your army did not strike it,
How could Jet-Kait have remained intact?
You went and shattered Afghanistan;
If you did not crush and pulverize it,
If you did not subdue it,
How could Bakünchö have remained intact?
While the hulking gray wolf lived,
You leveled men with your keen steel
And ruled every land you encountered.
We shattered them and took revenge.
We broke Altai and seized its valleys.
We routed the caravaners and took their tea.
While my lion-hearted uncle lived,
We hardened ourselves, sated with blood.
Throughout the world we were named “bloodthirsty.”
If told to take a cap, we cut off a head;
If told to drink water, we drank poison;
If told to spill blood, we spilled our fury.
We covered the valley’s waters with fat.
When together we struck the vengeful foe,
We laid even our own fathers low.
When we were driven into utter fury,
Khan Manas’s forty choros—
Not forty warriors, but forty companions,
Each of the forty had a different way,
All forty were famed champions who shattered the age.
Their horses grew fat and battle-ready;
Gathering around Manas,
They became renowned as the Forty.
When a lord thrust a spear, they flew like bullets;
When they attacked, they destroyed lives.
We slew the forty choros;
We did it because of what they themselves had done.
They spared no life, however one pleaded,
Those forty choros who attacked as one,
Whose knives were ever ready to slaughter.
Those forty choros went forth prepared,
And when they enraged us bitterly,
We destroyed the forty nobles
And made their women and girls weep.
From the forty courts of the forty choros,
We swept like wind and seized the ridge,
And wrought a mighty slaughter.
When they truly provoked our wrath,
We overthrew Abyke,
Sent Köbösh to the grave,
And showed every accursed enemy
The valor of gray wolves.
We anointed the white steel with blood.
Now tell the truth of your dire ordeals!
Tell of the saddlecloth you rode forth upon,
Tell of the valor that routed that host!”
When Seytek pressed him thus,
How could Choro remain silent?
If Külchoro refused to speak,
Could there ever be another like him?
“Fatherless brave Seytek, my son,
You would have me sing my song;
You would have me recount my scars.
You would have me begin the siege,
Hero, you would have me intensify the calamity.
You would hear my words,
Hero, you would have me vent my spirit!
You have brought this sorrow-laden head
To a halt at Kapka-Tash;
Why awaken the madness of long ago?
If I speak of my former days,
My son Seytek, wait a while,
For it may sound as if I boast.
If I speak of what lies ahead,
It may sound as though I am exulting.
Thinking on so many dire troubles,
I may seem carried away.
While my gray-wolf hero lived,
We broke through Kapchal and opened a road.
Without gathering people or mustering troops,
We attacked the Khagan’s China
And raided Beijing, taking horses.
Red gold and ruby stones,
Precious jewels we took.
From the long-legged Chinese we took artisans,
And we took surpassingly beautiful girls.
We stormed and shattered them and took their herds.
Cotton sashes and broad boots,
The great lord, khan of the monks—
We captured a khan named Eskara.
We broke Kyyas and captured the caravan.
With battle cries we fought for six months,
Against the swarming Chinese—
He spilled my blood upon the field,
He crushed my soul,
He tormented me while I yet lived,
Severed my arm at the shoulder,
And made my blood stream like water.
He robbed me of my strength
And poured out my blood like water.
While my ill-fated uncle lived,
Wherever I faced became a crimson fire;
I was a lion surpassing all mortals.
After my hero passed away,
I became no lion, but mere black earth.
Parted from my princely lion,
I became a grave whose crown had caved in.
I fell prey to cruel wrath
And was trampled into the black earth.
I became Kyyaz’s spoil,
A herdsman’s slave.
For twelve years
I tanned raw hides.
I danced like the Kalmyks,
I endured nights of bitter wrath
And somehow lived on without dying.
My forefather was the Chinese Chylaba;
Ask me no more of this humiliation.
With the hero gone from sight,
Both my shoulder blades were gouged.
Your uncle Kül, the lion of the world,
Was flayed by every kind of ordeal.
Everywhere I stepped was a deep pit;
Our great master was Kyyaz.
Condemned and disgraced,
Külchoro, brother of the noble hero,
Your uncle suffered such degradation.
Thinking of the days ahead,
We burn until we lose our senses.
“He has been left an orphan by the noble one,” we say,
And take courage from that thought.
“If he is a lion who takes after his father,
He will wage many battles,” we say.
When they truly provoked our wrath,
We laid Adybay and Kölbay low.
We anointed the blue steel with blood.
When our true fury was aroused,
Those two villains Chyybyl and Kochkor—
We laid both villains low.
When they roused our dreadful fury,
We all broke free of them.
Not six villains, but forty choros—
We cut off their heads with our swords.
We surrounded Koton and took its citadel.
We attacked its principal people,
Besieged them in anguish and took their land,
Then raided Künjüt and conquered its people.
While my sultan uncle lived,
We chased white deer and made them cattle,
And made the whole world submit.
We chased blue deer and made them cattle,
And visibly brought the earth under our rule.
At the word “enemy,” our spirits soared;
We shattered Jet-Kait and ruled it.
We broke through the cliffs and seized the valleys,
Overthrowing and capturing many khans.
Then, grieving through youthful folly,
I lost Taibuurul,
The wing on which I wheeled and flew.
A fire burned from my very core,
And my own kinsman turned stranger.
We had kicked together like foals,
And quarreled while nursing at the same breast.
But Kanchoro the swine rose as my enemy,
Broke both my arms,
And kicked my side out.
Raging worse than any enemy,
My own kin dealt me such torment.
My kinsman became my enemy,
An unshifting mountain within me.
My wrath will never melt away:
That wretched Kanchoro
Is my sworn enemy.
When the people gathered to bury him,
The confidant of the noble one,
Your forefather Manas’s companion,
The sorrowing hero Bakai remained.
While your princely father, the sultan, lived,
The elder Bakai did not die.
The people cried out and the nation lamented,
Yet we did not bury my khanly uncle.
Dust soared into the sky;
“The sovereign Bakai has died,” they said,
And the army surged in clouds of dust.
Fifty thousand animals led by mares
We did not slaughter for the lord’s funeral feast.
For valiant Bakai’s thunderous funeral
We did not hold rites like Kökötöy’s.
We arrayed the white-bearded elders,
And made his noble bones gleam like copper.
We had him washed with Zamzam water
And wrapped in cloth of gold.
We had him washed with kumis
And wrapped in brocade.
We dressed the daughters-in-law in mourning robes,
Letting the hems of their silken coats
Spread wide and touch the ground.
We dressed the maidens in red,
Letting the hems of their fine coats
Trail diagonally along the road.
The lion Bakai did not die;
The people did not witness his death.
Sixty thousand animals led by camels
Were offered as prizes,
And bright crimson fabrics
Were spread as funeral adornments.
Countless dark and fallow beasts
Were arrayed in ceremonial ranks.
Our forefather Bakai did not die;
Your heroic father Semetey
Did not bury Khan Bakai.
We did not remain after burying the prince.
For my heroic uncle Bakai,
We ask whether, if he returns to us, he will fight
And rescue the widows, orphans,
And the poor from bondage—
That is what we keep asking.
We wandered here as plunder,
Parted from the mighty lion.
We were captured and imprisoned,
And by a wrathful enemy
Bound without rope or cord.
We wandered, finding no escape.
Thinking Kyyaz would issue a decree,
We stand here helpless.
“A protector remains from the hero,” we say,
And make you our protector.
We came as slaves, sobbing and wasting away;
We came as bondwomen, taken as spoil.
I have longed to die from shame,
Yet I remain alive, my foal,
Because worthy Seytek lives.
I have longed to depart from shame,
Yet I remain here alive
Because Seytek, whom I need, lives.
From your princely father, gray-wolf Semetey,
From your lion-hearted father himself,
From the black eyes of the Karakhan line,
The broad land of Keң-Kol remained,
And the happy Kyrgyz people remained.
Riding colts and flying hunting birds,
They once lived in wild delight—
The poor Kyrgyz people remained,
